paras: The attempted lynching of Daniel Reed took place in Alexandria, Indiana, on the night of July 26, 1903, when a mob pursued a Black saloon porter accused of assaulting a man and a woman. The porter escaped in the darkness, and the episode was reported in two special dispatches the following day.

The porter worked at Tom Martin's saloon on the "east side" of Alexandria, according to the Louisville Courier-Journal. The Indianapolis Journal named him Daniel Reed, also printed "Reid," while the Courier-Journal called him a porter "known only as 'Pollock.'"

Both dispatches stated that the porter assaulted a man named Taylor, whom the Journal identified as Martin Taylor and said was cut, and the Courier-Journal described as "an old man." Mrs. Richard Hollis interfered and was in turn attacked, or in the Courier-Journal's word "beaten."
An "angry mob" then collected and went after him, in the Journal's account "with the intention of lynching" him. He was chased about a mile into the country before the pursuers lost him in the dark.
No report of the porter's capture, of any arrest of members of the mob, or of a court proceeding over the assaults appears in the coverage found.

Coverage came from two white dailies on July 28, each carrying a special dispatch from Alexandria dated July 27. The Indianapolis Journal headlined its item "Negro Chased by a Mob" and opened by crediting the porter's "fleetfootedness" with having "saved the town from a lynching." The Courier-Journal ran a shorter front-page paragraph, "Pursued By Indiana Mob," beside a report of Iowa farmers hunting a Black man accused of a razor assault and a notice of a Chautauqua conference on lynchings and the "mob spirit."
Both papers stated the assaults as fact and described the mob without comment. No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

The two dispatches named the porter differently, as Daniel Reed in Indianapolis and "Pollock" in Louisville, but agree on his workplace role, the people he was accused of attacking, and his escape, and appear to describe the same man.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Daniel Reed
bases: Both dispatches describe a crowd pursuing a Black porter after an alleged assault, A1 stating it meant to lynch him, and both say he escaped in the darkness, making this an attempted lynching (A1, A2).

A mob of citizens with no lawful authority pursued the porter over an alleged assault, with the stated intention of lynching him, but both reports say he escaped and neither reports anyone killed, so this was an attempted lynching, not a lynching (A1, A2).

Two separate special dispatches from Alexandria, in Indianapolis and Louisville papers, agree on the core event (a mob chased a Black saloon porter accused of assaulting a man named Taylor and Mrs. Richard Hollis, and he escaped in the dark), though they give him different names (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal special
accounts.gist: Daniel Reed, a 'colored saloon porter', cut Martin Taylor and attacked Mrs. Richard Hollis; an angry mob pursued him intending to lynch him, and he was lost in the darkness a mile into the country.

accounts.label: Courier-Journal special
accounts.gist: A 'negro porter known only as "Pollock"' of Tom Martin's saloon assaulted an old man named Taylor and beat Mrs. Hollis; a mob of enraged citizens pursued him until he escaped in the darkness.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal headlined it 'Negro Chased by a Mob', stated the assault as fact, and credited the porter's 'fleetfootedness' with having 'saved the town from a lynching', without comment on the mob.

The Courier-Journal ran a short front-page item, 'Pursued By Indiana Mob', beside an Iowa manhunt report and notice of a Chautauqua conference on lynchings and the 'mob spirit', stating the assault as fact.

conflicts.note: Same incident, same place, same accusers in both dispatches; the two names almost certainly refer to one man, and neither source is clearly better.
